etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ripe, rype, from Old English rīpe (“ripe, mature”), from Proto-West Germanic *rīpī, from Proto-Germanic *rīpijaz, *rīpiz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁reyb- (“to snatch”). Cognate with West Frisian ryp (“ripe”), Dutch rijp (“ripe”), German reif (“ripe”). Related to reap.

definitions.definition: (of fruits, vegetables, seeds etc.) Ready for reaping or gathering; having attained perfection; mature.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “(please specify the page number)”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: So mayst thou live, till, like ripe fruit, thou drop / Into thy mother's lap.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, David Van Tassel, Lee DeHaan, “Wild Plants to the Rescue”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3:
quote.text: Plant breeding is always a numbers game. […] The wild species we use are rich in genetic variation, […]. In addition, we are looking for rare alleles, so the more plants we try, the better. These rarities may be new mutations, or they can be existing ones that are neutral—or are even selected against—in a wild population. A good example is mutations that disrupt seed dispersal, leaving the seeds on the heads long after they are ripe.

definitions.definition: (of foods) Advanced to the state of fitness for use; mellow.
(figuratively) Having attained its full development; mature; perfected.

quote.citation: 1623, William Shakespeare, The Life of King Henry the Eighth:
quote.text: He was a scholar, and a ripe and good one.

quote.citation: 1850, [Alfred, Lord Tennyson], In Memoriam, London: Edward Moxon, […], →OCLC, Canto XLI, page 64:
quote.text: And so may Place retain us still,⁠And he the much-beloved again,⁠A lord of large experience, trainTo riper growth the mind and will:  […]

quote.citation: 1895, Henry James, The Altar of the Dead:
quote.text: She was a feature of that piety, but even at the ripe stage of acquaintance in which they occasionally arranged to meet at a concert or to go together to an exhibition she was not a feature of anything else.
When you're ripeYou'll bleed out of control

definitions.definition: (archaic) Maturated or suppurated; ready to discharge. (said of sores, tumors, etc.)
Ready for action or effect; prepared.

quote.citation: 1705, J[oseph] Addison, Remarks on Several Parts of Italy, &c. in the Years 1701, 1702, 1703, London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: while things were just ripe for a war
I am not ripe to pass sentence on the gravest public bodies.

quote.citation: 1910, Theodore C. Williams, The Aeneid, translation of Aeneis by Virgil, Book IV Chapter 28:
quote.text: nor was the doom / of guilty deed, but of a hapless wight / to sudden madness stung, ere ripe to die, / therefore the Queen of Hades had not shorn / the fair tress from her forehead, nor assigned / that soul to Stygian dark.
But the time is ripe for changes. There's a growing feeling. That taking a chance on a new kind of vision is due

definitions.definition: Like ripened fruit in ruddiness and plumpness.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1606, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of King Lear”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Those happy smilets, / That played on her ripe lip.

quote.citation: 1981, Daniel Curzon, Human Warmth & Other Stories‎[2], →ISBN, page 18:
quote.text: He looked back once at the waving hands, the mother's glowing, ripe cheeks.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: Alonso: And Trinculo is reeling-ripe: where should they / Find this grand liquor that hath gilded them? / How cam'st thou in this pickle?

definitions.definition: (law) Of a conflict between parties, having developed to a stage where the conflict may be reviewed by a court of law.

quote.citation: 2004, Kenneth F. Warren, Administrative Law in the Political System‎[3], →ISBN, page 427:
quote.text: Problems emerge in judging whether a case is ripe, however, when contested general agency directives are issued that are not aimed at specific parties.

quote.citation: 2004, Colum McCann, Fishing the Sloe-Black River‎[4], →ISBN, page 141:
quote.text: Dolores, giving her a bath yesterday, said she was a bit ripe under the armpits.

definitions.definition: (agriculture) A fruit or vegetable which has ripened.

quote.citation: 1993, Paul J. Dosal, Doing Business with the Dictators‎[5], →ISBN, page 76:
quote.text: When he realized that the ripes would not make it back to Selma, Zemurray offered a free bunch of bananas to any telegraph operator who notified local grocers that he was coming through with a shipment of bananas.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene viii]:
quote.text: […]  he answer'd, "Do not so; / Slubber not business for my sake, Bassanio, / But stay the very riping of the time; /  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ripe, from Latin ripa.
